title: The grocer and the parrot (Mathnawi, Book 1)
text: Rumi's heading: حکایت بقال و طوطی و روغن ریختن طوطی در دکان ('The story of the grocer and the parrot, and the parrot's spilling the oil in the shop'). The tale ends at 262; from 263 Rumi speaks in his own voice.

title: Rumi on mathnawi-1-grocer-and-parrot (author_moral)
text: 'Do not measure the affairs of the pure by yourself, though lion and milk are alike in writing' (263). The people laughed at the parrot's analogy, 'for it supposed the wearer of the patched robe to be like itself' (262). (Claude's translation.)

title: Housam on mathnawi-1-grocer-and-parrot (reader)
text: The parrot represents the material world: beautiful, in sound and in looks. Then something stressful: the beauty, not equipped for it, breaks and withdraws, until it sees another and assumes they are the same.

data.supported_by: 247-249 (voice, colour, speech), 250 (it bolts in fear), 253 (silence), 261 (it reads its own story into the dervish)

title: Claude on mathnawi-1-grocer-and-parrot (claude)
text: The text supports each step of Housam's reading. A refinement: the parrot may be the outward sense, the faculty that knows only form and sound, more than the world itself; Rumi's own lines point this way ('the sense of this world is the ladder of this world', 303; 'the letter is a vessel and the meaning in it is like water', 296). What Housam's reading adds to Rumi's stated moral: it shows what the parrot measures with, its own wound. A caution: the parrot is not one fixed symbol; later in the same book it is 'the parrot of the soul' (1575), the spirit caged in the body.

title: Claude on parrot-s1 (claude)
text: The text supports this: the grocer's dealings with the world pass through the bird, and it is what makes his shop bright. With this reading the centre of the story moves from the bird to the man. What we hold: the parrot is the grocer's blessing and his window on the world; it has beauty and speech, and nothing yet says it has understanding.

title: Claude on parrot-s2 (plain_sense)
text: The master had gone home and the parrot kept the shop. A cat sprang into the shop after a mouse; the parrot, in fear for its life, fled to one side and spilled the bottles of rose oil. The master came back and sat down at ease, like a lord; he saw the shop full of oil and his clothes greasy, and struck the parrot on the head; it became bald from the blow. (Claude's translation.)
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Housam on parrot-s2 (reader)
text: He took the beauty and the blessings for granted, then broke the blessings.

title: Claude on parrot-s2 (claude)
text: Both halves are in the text. One thing the text adds: the parrot's failure was fear; it fled 'in fear for its life' and had no thought for the shop it guarded. The blessing was real, and it was never equal to the trust placed in it. What we hold: the blessing is lost through the owner's anger over a lesser thing. The oil was spilled by fear; the parrot was silenced by the blow.

title: Section 3: silence and remorse

data.voice_in_text: the narrator, with the grocer speaking in 254-255

by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Claude on parrot-s3 (plain_sense)
text: For some days the parrot did not speak. The grocer sighed with remorse and tore his beard: 'Alas, the sun of my blessing has gone under the cloud. Would that my hand had been broken at the moment I struck that sweet-tongued one.' He gave gifts to every dervish so that his bird might find its speech. After three days and nights, bewildered and wretched, he sat in the shop in despair, showing the bird every kind of thing so that it might begin to speak. (Claude's translation.)
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Housam on parrot-s3 (reader)
text: He began to weep, wishing and doing everything he could to get back what he had.
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Claude on parrot-s3 (claude)
text: Exact. He names what he lost with the Qur'an's word for a favour from Allah, niʿmat, and knows its worth only now. His efforts are of two kinds, giving (256) and coaxing (258), and neither works; the cure, when it comes, is neither bought nor arranged, and he has reached despair (257) before it arrives. What we hold: remorse and effort do not restore the blessing by themselves; they bring the grocer to the point where he has nothing left to try.

title: Section 4: the bald dervish and the parrot's question

data.voice_in_text: the narrator, with the parrot speaking in 261

by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Claude on parrot-s4 (plain_sense)
text: A dervish passed by, bare-headed, his head hairless as the back of a bowl. At once the parrot began to speak and called out to him, as the rational do: 'Why, bald one, have you joined the bald? Did you too spill oil from the bottle?' The people laughed at its analogy, for it supposed the wearer of the patched robe to be like itself. (Claude's translation.)
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Housam on parrot-s4 (reader)
text: Then a dervish arrives to restore the beauty, by reflecting an image that allowed the parrot to open up.
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Claude on parrot-s4 (claude)
text: This reading sees something Rumi's stated moral passes over, and the two need to be held together. The dervish is a mirror: he does nothing; the parrot sees its own likeness in him and speaks. What the mirror restores is speech; what the parrot says is a mistake (262). So the same moment is a healing and an error: Housam's reading holds the healing, and Rumi's next couplet takes up the error. It meets al-Jilani in the heart case: 'make me your mirror; come close, for you will see in yourself what you do not see far from me'. What we hold: the blessing is restored by the sight of a friend of God, freely and without his doing anything; the one restored still sees only the outward likeness.
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Section 5: do not measure the pure by yourself
text: In Persian script the words for lion and milk are written with the same letters, شیر.

data.voice_in_text: Rumi, in his own voice for the first time: the tale has ended

by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Rumi on parrot-s5 (author_moral)
text: 'Do not measure the affairs of the pure by yourself, though lion and milk are alike in writing. For this reason the whole world went astray: few came to know the Substitutes of God. They claimed equality with the prophets; they supposed the saints to be like themselves. They said: we are human and they are human; we and they alike are bound to sleep and food. In their blindness they did not know that between them is a difference without end.' (Claude's translation.)
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Housam on parrot-s5 (reader)
text: One can nourish you, and the other you nourish it.
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Housam on parrot-s5 (reader)
text: The lion and the milk are both nourishing, and a cure for different ailments. (This revises his first reading, where one nourished and the other was fed.) And of the two: what looks like loss may veil a light; a hidden dawn inside the night.

data.supported_by: 263; Rumi's own image of the cupper's lancet at 244 and the arrowhead at 309

by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Claude on parrot-s5 (claude)
text: Housam's first reading takes the lion and the milk by what each does to you; Claude first read the lion as a predator. Housam's revised reading fits the couplet better, since Rumi calls neither one bad: the pure cure in two ways, one gentle and one severe. The milk is the cure that looks like a gift; the lion is the cure that looks like loss. Rumi supports this three couplets before the story: 'the child trembles at the sting of the cupper's lancet; the loving mother at that moment is glad' (244). Rumi does not say which of the two is the saint; the text leaves it open, and so does this record. What we hold: the pure cure in two ways, and the severe cure looks like harm to the one who measures by himself.
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Section 6: like forms, different fruits
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Rumi on parrot-s6 (author_moral)
text: 'Both kinds of zanbur fed from the same place, but from that one came the sting and from this other, honey. Both kinds of deer ate grass and drank water: from this one came dung and from that one pure musk. Both reeds drank from one watering-place: this one is empty and that one full of sugar. See a hundred thousand such likenesses; see the difference between them, a seventy years' road. This one eats and filth comes from him; that one eats and it becomes entirely the light of God... If the two forms resemble each other, so they may: bitter water and sweet water are both clear. Who but the one who has taste can tell them apart? Find him; he knows the sweet water from the brackish.' (Claude's translation.)
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Housam on parrot-s6 (reader)
text: Don't judge the form by what you see; a different form hides a different sea.
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Claude on parrot-s6 (claude)
text: Housam's reading of the lion and the milk as two cures holds for 263 and does not hold for the pairs of this section, where every pair is set as good against bad (honey and sting, musk and dung, the light of God and filth, an angel and a demon). Rumi's point here is that the same food yields opposite fruit, and the difference lies in the one who eats. The gathering of opposites returns in Rumi's own words at 298. Rumi's claim in 275 is about the same form: the likeness is real, and it is on the surface. What we hold: two readings stand side by side. The pure differ among themselves, and each is a cure for something (Housam, on 263); and two things that look alike and feed alike can be opposite in what they are, known only by taste (Rumi, 268-276).
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Staying with the bees (268)
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Housam on parrot-s6-bees (reader)
text: Again the analogy: the same field, the same type of bees. They leave together but come back with different results. And who gets the sting, and who gets the honey? (With the song's lines: don't weigh light by your own dark; a saint may wear a common mark; two forms stand beneath one sky, yet one is ash and one is a spark.)
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Claude on parrot-s6-bees (claude)
text: One correction from the Persian: Rumi says 'both kinds' (har do gun), and his word zanbur covers the wasp and the honeybee, so in his text they are two kinds that look alike and feed alike; the song's 'two bees' hides this. 'Don't weigh light by your own dark' is a faithful rendering of 263. Housam's question, who gets the sting and who gets the honey, turns from the giver to the receiver. Rumi does not ask it in this couplet; he answers it elsewhere: the water of the Nile was blood to the Egyptian and water to the people of Moses (4:33; also 3:3028), and the sting itself can be the cure (1:244; 1:3002). What we hold: the difference between two like things lies first in what they are (Rumi, 268), and then in who comes to them (Housam, with Rumi 4:33). The same source gives each person according to what he brings.
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: 'Find him' (276)
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Rumi on parrot-s6-find-him (author_moral)
text: 'Who but the possessor of taste (sahib-i dhawq) can tell them apart? Find him; he knows the sweet water from the brackish.' Rumi does not say the eye can learn to tell: he sends the reader to a person. (Claude's translation.)
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Housam on parrot-s6-find-him (reader)
text: The one who has tasted both sweet and salt is the one who can guide you through this maze of salt and sweet. And imagine: too much or too little of salt or sweet can be harmful.
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Claude on parrot-s6-find-him (claude)
text: The first sentence is what the couplet says: knowing by taste means having drunk, and 'both' is right, since one who has known only the sweet has nothing to compare it with. Measure is Housam's addition: the couplet speaks of telling the two apart, not of how much of each. But the guide as one who knows the dose is in the passage: 'seek the health of this sense from the physician; seek the health of that sense from the Beloved' (304). The Qur'an supports the use of both seas (35:12). One limit from the Persian: the word in 274 and 276 is shura, brackish water and barren salt-soil, not table salt, and here Rumi means it as the worse of the two. What we hold: the difference between like things is known by tasting, so one must find a guide who has tasted both; on Housam's reading the guide also knows how much of each a person can bear.
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Section 7: magic and miracle; the ape
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Rumi on parrot-s7 (author_moral)
text: 'He has measured magic against miracle and supposes both to rest on trickery. The magicians, out of rivalry with Moses, took up a staff like his staff. Between this staff and that staff is a deep difference; from this act to that act is a mighty road... Whatever a man does, the ape does too... He supposes: I have done as he did. How should that quarrelsome one know the difference? This one acts by command, and that one for the sake of quarrel.' (Claude's translation.)
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Housam on parrot-s7 (reader)
text: One had a divine snake, and the others are fools doing magic tricks with a real deadly snake. In life, the doctor and the actors: when they arrive on the scene to save the life of Pharaoh, one shows who is the King of kings, with real medicine for what ails Pharaoh, where the others are there to confuse and to appease an ego.
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Claude on parrot-s7 (claude)
text: Rumi's section names only the magicians and Moses; Housam brings in Pharaoh, and the Qur'an's telling supports each part: Moses is sent to Pharaoh as a cure offered to the patient (79:17-19; 20:44); what ails Pharaoh is the self (79:24); the magicians serve that self and ask for a reward (7:113-114; 26:44). 'Command against quarrel' is Rumi's own line (284): the doctor is sent, the actors are hired. One detail differs in the Qur'an: the magicians' snakes were not real (20:66); the real serpent was the staff of Moses (7:117), so the deadly real thing was on the doctor's side. The magicians were the first to recognise the real medicine and fell in prostration (7:120): those who knew the taste of fakery best knew at once that this was not it. The ape is the parrot again: it copies what it sees and supposes 'I have done as he did' (283). What we hold: two may arrive at the same sickbed with the same instruments; one is sent to heal the patient and the other is hired to please him. An act is known by its source and not its form.
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Section 8: the hypocrite and the believer; the name and the meaning
text: Two half-lines are Qur'an: 'with Him is the Mother of the Book' (13:39) and 'between them is a barrier they do not overpass' (55:20).
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Rumi on parrot-s8 (author_moral)
text: 'The hypocrite stands with the one in accord at prayer out of rivalry, not out of need... The ugliness of that bad name is not from the letters; the bitterness of that sea-water is not from the vessel. The letter is a vessel and the meaning in it is like water; the sea of meaning is with Him who has the Mother of the Book. The bitter sea and the sweet sea in this world: between them is a barrier they do not overpass. And yet both of these flow from one source. Pass beyond them both; go to their source.' (Claude's translation.)
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Housam on parrot-s8 (reader)
text: Pass beyond both and go to the source, for they flow from the same source. The farther we are away from the source, the uglier and saltier the world becomes. Don't blame the ugliness or the salt, but the vessel's distance from the source.
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54

title: Claude on parrot-s8 (claude)
text: The first sentence is Rumi's own (298). The rest gives a reason Rumi does not state here. It agrees with him on the source: his word is asl, the word of the Mathnawi's fourth couplet ('everyone who has stayed far from his source seeks again the time of his union', 1:4), so Housam's reading ties this passage back to the reed's lament. It agrees that distance darkens: al-Jilani says the heart 'blackens through its distance from the light'. It differs on the vessel: Rumi clears the vessel outright (295), and Housam puts the cause in a third thing, distance; Rumi stops one step earlier and does not say how one source became two. A caution Rumi keeps: 'between them is a barrier they do not overpass' (297); in this world the two do not mix, and the oneness is at the source. What we hold: sweet and bitter are one at their source and separate in this world; the letter is only a vessel; on Housam's reading, bitterness measures how far a thing has come from its source, and the cure is to travel back.
by: Claude, from the section-by-section reading of the story with Housam (2026-10-03), entered in v54
